In 'Daughters & Sons' (Chapter: 'Daughters and Sons'), what is the central teaching on practice?

In this section of *Daughters & Sons*, the teaching focuses on direct observation of the mind: *"by Ajahn Jayasaro Many years ago before I was ordained as a monk, I believed that wisdom came from experience."* The central guidance is to step back from the habitual impulse to control or fix present experience, and instead cultivate a spacious, non-reactive presence. When we investigate thoughts and feelings without identification (*anattā*), their grip on the heart naturally dissolves. It is like It is like a small boat floating on a calm mountain lake beneath an open sky. Rest in that clear, unentangled knowing.

In 'Daughters & Sons' (Daughters and Sons), how should a meditator handle restless thoughts and mental chatter?

The text reflects: *"As for my mind, it was more and more like that of a hungry ghost, constantly worrying about food: “Will I get anything to eat today or not?” Whether my stomach would be empty or full depended on the kindness of fellow human beings."* Thoughts are merely passing mental formations (*saṅkhāra*); they have no solid core unless we feed them with belief. When a thought arises, simply recognize it as 'thinking, thinking' without jumping into the storyline. It is like It is like a deep ocean holding waves on its surface while remaining utterly still below. Be the vast, open sky through which thoughts pass like harmless clouds.

In 'Daughters & Sons' (Daughters and Sons), how are we advised to relate to suffering and emotional tension?

The text instructs: *"But she accepted the suffering because she believed that there was something worthwhile in it, and that something was me."* Rather than resisting discomfort or becoming identified with it as 'my pain', the Forest Tradition guides us to bring gentle, interested awareness directly to the feeling. Observe that tension is an impermanent, conditioned phenomenon arising in awareness. It is like It is like letting muddy water in a glass sit undisturbed until it becomes crystal clear. Allow the knot of tension to unwind naturally in spacious presence.

The text teaches: *"After a while, I realized that I gained the opportunity to practice Buddhism, in order to develop a true inner refuge, because my parents had provided me with a stable, dependable external refuge when I was young."* This reflection invites us to look past superficial conventions into the living reality of the present moment. By cultivating patience, virtue, and clear discernment, the mind discovers an unshakable inner refuge. It is like It is like opening the window shutters of a stuffy room to let the fresh mountain breeze flow in. Walk the noble path with confidence and peace.
